Everything here turns on how many customers you lose when the price goes up. Nobody knows that number for your cafe — the figure used comes from research on eating out as a whole.

Your supplier put wholesale prices up {shock}%.
A 4% rise plus dropping low-margin lines

A shop's customers can often buy the same item elsewhere, so a price rise costs more orders here than in a trade where people come for you specifically. How much more is the thing nobody has measured for your shop.
Put prices up on a handful of lines for two weeks and watch what happens to those lines against the rest. Your own numbers from the last time you raised prices work too.
Loyal customers, an awkward shop to replace, or competitors raising prices too.
Our judgement: customers who could shop elsewhere, with some effort.
The research figure for customers who can buy the identical item elsewhere.
Depends on how much dropping low-margin lines cuts your cost of goods (about {red} points here) and how many {unit} leave with those lines ({loss}%). Neither is measured from your shop.
Costs take about three weeks to rise — the stock on your shelves was bought at the old price. Customers react to a new price within a week or two.
The research quoted measures customers switching between brands on the same shelf, which is easier than switching shops. It sets the top of the range rather than the middle.

Demand for appointments is up {shock}%, and your diary has a ceiling.
A 5% rise plus shifting the mix

There is no published figure for how salon clients respond to a price rise — not a weak one, none we could use honestly. Every setting on this control is our judgement, so your own test is worth more here than in any other trade.
Raise the price of one service, or for new clients only, and count rebookings over six weeks.
A loyal client base who book with you personally.
Our judgement for an appointment business with real switching costs.
Stress case: clients who treat it as a commodity and shop on price.
Your diary has a ceiling, so some of the {unit} a price rise costs you were being turned away anyway. That is why raising prices costs less here than the price sensitivity alone suggests.

Depends on how much shifting the mix cuts your cost per appointment (about {red} points here), how much it lifts the average ticket, and how many {unit} leave with the discounts ({loss}%). None is measured from your salon.
Clients on a six-week cycle only meet a new price at their next visit, so the reaction arrives over a couple of weeks rather than at once.

We found no published figure for personal-care services that could be used honestly. Every setting on the price control is our judgement. The retail studies listed are only the reference points our range was positioned against.
